title: From live birds to clay targets
summary: How shooters moved from live pigeons to glass balls and then to clay targets in the 19th century, and what that path left in today's sport.

body.html: Modern clay shooting grew out of hunting. Hunters wanted to practise out of season and to compete under equal conditions. In the 18th and 19th centuries, especially in England, they shot at live pigeons released from small boxes in front of the shooter.

That era left words we still use. In English the throwing machine is still called a trap, the old name of the box that held the bird. The call «pull» is often linked to the cord that was pulled to open the box. People like this story, but there is no written record of it.

Live-bird shooting drew more and more criticism. The birds were also expensive, and each one flew differently. Glass balls became an alternative: a simple device threw them into the air, and they shattered when hit. They came from England, but nobody knows exactly when they were first used there. They reached the USA in about 1866, and there glass-ball shooting had its heyday from about 1877 to 1883.

Glass had a serious drawback: after each match the field was covered in sharp splinters, and farm animals grazing there could cut themselves. The breakthrough came in 1880, when an American inventor patented a flat, saucer-shaped target of baked clay. That is where the English name clay pigeon comes from.

The first targets really were baked clay. Later makers switched to a mix of pitch (a black, tar-like binder) and limestone, and most targets are still made that way. Pitch-free biodegradable targets exist too. But the name stuck, and in English the whole sport is called clay shooting.

Over time live-bird shooting disappeared or was banned in many countries. In Great Britain a law of 1921, the Captive Birds Shooting (Prohibition) Act, banned it. In 2003 the FITASC General Assembly (the meeting of all its member federations) voted to suspend all events that used live animals as targets.

Today the rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ put people's safety and care for nature first, and shooting at live animals is not allowed. The hunting roots stay in the targets: they fly like game (the birds a hunter would shoot), but nobody hunts anything.

key_points.html: Clay shooting grew out of hunting and live-pigeon shooting.
Glass balls became a common alternative to live birds in the 19th century.
The clay target was patented in the USA in 1880.
The English words trap and «pull» are often traced back to those times.
In 2003 FITASC suspended all events that used live animals as targets.

did_you_know.html: Targets have not been made of clay for a long time, yet in English they are still called clay pigeons, or simply clays.

quiz.q: What did shooters use as targets before clay ones?

options.text: Paper targets pinned to a wall
Glass balls, and earlier live pigeons
Metal plates fixed to a frame

quiz.explain: First came live pigeons, then glass balls, and from 1880 clay targets.

quiz.q: When and where was the clay target patented?
quiz.explain: An American inventor patented the clay target in 1880. In 1921 a British law banned live-bird shooting.

quiz.q: Why did glass balls go out of use?

options.text: Sharp glass was left all over the field
They were far too big to miss
A federation banned them by rule

quiz.explain: Glass left dangerous splinters, and the clay target solved that problem.
